# Scientific journal and peer review (`scientific_journal`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/communication.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Communication & information (`communication`)
- Deps: needs printing_press; helped by postal_system, scientific_academy, reproducibility_open_publication
- Core idea: A periodical that prints short reports of new observations and experiments, dated and with enough detail of method that others can repeat them. Priority goes to whoever publishes first, so discoverers publish instead of keeping secrets, and readers can test and criticise. An editor gathers reports through correspondence; later, referees judge submissions before printing. Minimum: a regular schedule, an editor, a correspondence network, method and measurement in each report, and openness to authors who are not members.
- Pitfalls:
  - Thinking peer review began in 1665: the Royal Society's Committee of Papers selected articles from 1752; its archive of specialist referees’ reports begins in the 1830s
  - Believing publication proves a result true: it only makes it open to being checked
  - Publishing results without method and measurements: nobody can repeat them
  - Expecting craftsmen to share trade secrets: they need priority or patent protection first
- History: islamic: c. 997 – al-Biruni and Ibn Sina exchange written questions and answers on physics, an example of open scholarly controversy, but no periodical; europe: 5 January 1665 – Journal des sçavans, Paris; 6 March 1665 Philosophical Transactions, edited by Henry Oldenburg; 1682 Acta Eruditorum, Leipzig; 1752 Royal Society Committee of Papers; 1869 Nature; americas: 1818 – American Journal of Science; 1880 Science
- Read:
  - Aileen Fyfe, Noah Moxham, Julie McDougall-Waters & Camilla Mørk Røstvik, A History of Scientific Journals: Publishing at the Royal Society, 1665–2015 (2022)
  - David A. Kronick, A History of Scientific and Technical Periodicals (1962)
